subject: Abundance As a Covariate to Assess Competition

messages.author: 0c69c6d399345fab
messages.subject: Abundance As a Covariate to Assess Competition
parts:
Hi fellow Unmarkers,

Quick question. I've used the 2-species model as described by Richmond et al. 2010 to model coexistence when one species is thought to be dominant and the other subordinate. The novelty of this model, is that it allows the user to model parameters for  coexistence, while simultaneously accounting for how the detection of one species might affect the other. 

However, what about abundance? Is it worth modeling raw species count data in a GLM format (assuming a Poisson distribution obviously)  as a function of the raw abundance of another? In this scenario, 
the environmental variables that best described changes in the occupancy of both species could still be incorporated  while also including the abundance of a potential competitor.  Obviously, the biggest flaw here is that detection, and its influences on the parameter of interest cannot be modeled. Ultimately, I would be assuming that all zeros, were in fact true zeros. However, in my case, detection probabilities for my target species were fairly high under the single-season model, so I would assume that if I presented my argument, well, that a reviewer wouldn't be as likely to flag me on it. 

Abundance, as we all know, plays a tremendous role in determining the strength of biotic interactions, and there in lies my interest of pursuing this particular jaunt down the black hole that is "research".


Also, an aside, I'd love to use Royle's N-Mixture model to pursue something like this, but my data unfortunately is spatially and not temporally replicated. Blah.... :(


Cheers,

Josh

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Abundance As a Covariate to Assess Competition
parts:
Hi Josh,

I think it would be easy to formulate an abundance-based model like the ones by Richmond et al. (2010) and Waddle et al. (2010), inside of the binomial N-mixture framework, especially using the BUGS language. As far as I know, this hasn't been done so far (kind of surprising!).

However, I wouldn't feel comfortable to applying such a model to your data, for the reason you say (spatial, not not temporal reps).

So, I don't know, either you are stuck to ignoring the abundance information, but accounting for detection in an occupancy model. Or, you could model the counts in a two-species Poisson GLMM, but then have to ignore detection. Not sure what I'd do for a paper, but for exploratory purposes I'd probably to both.

Best regards  ---- Marc

Marc,

Thanks for the reply. At this point, this is truly exploratory (the paper has already been accepted for publication). A reviewer was concerned about the loss of the abundance data, and how that might skew inferences regarding coexistence which lead to me to posting this thought on the unmarked board.

Thanks!

-Josh
